name: Irkalla
description:
Irkalla takes its name from the Mesopotamian underworld, and the residents who coined it had a sense of humor about their situation. The northern half of old Irving Park — the quiet half, with its historic greystones and tree-lined streets — was absorbed into a Vantage Meridian residential development zone in Year 9. The corporation gutted the buildings, kept the facades, and filled them with climate-controlled Tier 3-4 housing units. From the outside, the greystones look exactly as they did a century ago. From the inside, they are corporate product. The trees were replaced with synthetic equivalents that require no maintenance and produce no allergens. The result is beautiful and completely dead — a museum of a neighborhood, preserved in corporate amber.

The southern half was not so lucky. Too close to the Kennedy Expressway interchange — now a maglev junction called the Switchback — the southern blocks became transit infrastructure. Buildings were demolished or absorbed into the junction's support structure. What remained between the pylons and the maglev tracks became a squatter settlement that calls itself the Understory, home to maintenance workers who service the Switchback and the unofficial economy that feeds them. The Understory is loud, oily, perpetually vibrating from train traffic overhead, and completely invisible to the people riding those trains.

The split between north and south Irkalla is physical and absolute. A corporate security barrier — officially a 'transit safety perimeter' — runs along what used to be Irving Park Road, separating the preserved greystones from the squatter pylons. Crossing requires either a Tier 3+ access credential or knowledge of the seventeen gaps in the barrier that the Understory residents maintain and the corporate security AI pretends not to notice. This arrangement suits everyone: Vantage Meridian gets to report zero unauthorized crossings, the Understory gets to exist, and the barrier gets to be a metaphor for everything wrong with the tier system.

The name stuck because Irkalla, in mythology, was a place you could enter but never leave. The Understory residents appreciate the irony. The Tier 3 residents in the greystones don't get the reference, because their neural interfaces auto-filter cultural content below their engagement profile.

sights: Historic greystone facades concealing corporate-standard interiors — architecture as costume
The Switchback maglev junction overhead, trains screaming through every ninety seconds
The security barrier along the old Irving Park Road line — concrete, sensor mesh, and corporate signage
Understory settlements built between maglev pylons, improvised structures vibrating with each train pass
Synthetic trees in the north that never lose their leaves and never look quite right
Maintenance workers in Switchback coveralls crossing through barrier gaps at shift change
sounds: Maglev trains — the dominant sound in both halves, inescapable, rhythmic, brain-reshaping
The north: curated silence underneath the train noise, corporate ambient masking
The south: industrial clanging, welding, the constant labor of keeping the junction functional
The barrier itself hums at a frequency designed to be uncomfortable to unaugmented hearing
smells: The north smells like nothing — air scrubbed to corporate specification
The south smells like maglev lubricant, hot metal, and the cooking fires of people who live between machines
Ozone from the junction — sharp, constant, the smell of infrastructure
atmosphere.feel: Irkalla feels like two cities pressed together with a wall between them. The north is uncanny in its preservation — walking past those greystones triggers something ancestral, a recognition of home that dissolves when you realize the windows don't open. The south vibrates. Literally. The maglev shakes the ground, the pylons, the teeth in your skull. Living in the Understory means learning to think between trains.

demographics: North: approximately 15,000 Tier 3-4 residents in corporate-managed housing. South (Understory): approximately 30,000 Tier 1 and untier-ed workers, predominantly transit maintenance crews and their families. The two populations share a zip code and nothing else.
dangers: The security barrier — crossing without credentials risks detention or worse
Maglev proximity — the Understory has regular casualties from train turbulence and falling debris
Corporate surveillance in the north — every greystone is a monitoring station
Structural instability in the Understory — buildings between pylons were never meant to be buildings
The vibration itself — long-term residents develop neurological symptoms the corporate health reports don't acknowledge
opportunities: Barrier gaps as transit routes between corporate and ungoverned territory
Switchback maintenance access — workers who know the junction know every route in and out of the northwest districts
The greystones' corporate networks are accessible from the Understory if you know which pylon carries the fiber
Understory mechanics who can repair anything that moves, no questions asked
story_hooks: A Tier 3 greystone resident has been passing data through a barrier gap to an Understory contact — and someone corporate has noticed
The maglev junction is developing unexplained routing errors that are diverting trains through unauthorized corridors — sabotage or infrastructure decay?
An Understory elder remembers the original Irving Park before the split and is recording oral histories that contradict the corporate version of the rezoning
frequented_by: Vantage Meridian residential tenants who never leave the north side
Transit maintenance crews commuting between the Understory and the Switchback
Smugglers using barrier gaps to move goods between corporate and ungoverned zones
Operators who need access to the maglev network's physical infrastructure
